options: Its recursive member references the CTE by its own name
It uses GROUP BY
It contains more than one JOIN
It is defined with a special RECURSIVE keyword
questions.explain: The self-reference in the second part of the UNION ALL is what makes the CTE recursive.

questions.q: What is the anchor member of a recursive CTE?
options: The starting point — the first part, before UNION ALL
The final row returned by the whole query
A required WHERE clause on the outer SELECT
A synonym for the recursive member
questions.explain: In the BOM example, the anchor is the top-level assembly's direct components at Level 0.

questions.q: How does SQL Server know when to stop repeating the recursive member?
options: It stops automatically once a pass produces no new rows
It always stops after exactly 3 passes
You must manually specify the number of levels in advance
It never stops on its own — an explicit STOP statement is required
questions.explain: This automatic termination is exactly what lets a recursive CTE walk hierarchies of unknown depth.

questions.q: Why must the anchor and recursive members be joined with UNION ALL instead of UNION?
options: T-SQL's recursive CTE syntax actually disallows UNION's deduplication here — UNION ALL is required
UNION ALL is just a stylistic preference with no real requirement
UNION would run faster, so it's always preferred over UNION ALL
UNION can only combine two SELECT statements, not CTEs
questions.explain: This is a hard syntax requirement for recursive CTEs, not just a performance recommendation.

questions.q: What real-world problem does the BillOfMaterials recursive CTE example solve?
options: Walking an arbitrary number of levels deep through assemblies made of components, some of which are themselves assemblies
Counting the total number of products in the database
Finding the average price of all products
Removing duplicate rows from a table
questions.explain: A regular (non-recursive) query can't walk an unknown number of hierarchy levels — that's exactly what recursion solves.
